messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 36
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Retail Worker
  trauma_type: Man-made disaster
  pcl5: 59

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Proximity: Physical proximity, Moral Violation: People misbehaving, Tactile (Texture): A specific texture associated with the event
  Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Thinking: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
  Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame, More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mark, a thirty-six-year-old retail worker who lives with his wife in a mid-sized Midwestern town, carries a scar on his right forearm that he tells himself is from a childhood bicycle accident. In truth, the scar is from a box cutter blade he pressed into his own skin six months after the gas explosion that tore through his department store on a Saturday afternoon in early December. He has never told his wife the real origin of the scar, and when she brushes against it in bed he flinches not from pain but from the shame that washes over him, a shame that has become inextricable from the memory itself.

The explosion happened during the holiday rush. Mark was helping a customer at the register near the home-goods aisle when a gas line ruptured in the stockroom. The blast came as a single tearing sound, then a pressure wave that knocked him sideways. In the seconds that followed, people began to run—not all of them toward the exits. He remembers a woman in a red coat pushing an elderly man to the ground to get past him. He remembers a teenage boy grabbing a cash drawer off a counter that had fractured open. He remembers the sound of glass shattering into a fine grit, and then, as he crawled toward the emergency door, his palm pressed against something that felt like wet, oversized sandpaper—a texture he later identified as fire-retardant ceiling tile that had crumbled and soaked through with something that was either water or worse. That texture, gritty and damp against his skin, is one of three things that can now stop him mid-sentence, his hand frozen in the air as if the surface is still there.

His memory of the event does not unfold as a story. It comes as three static images, each one perfectly clear and utterly separate: the customer’s face going slack before the noise hit, the red coat shoving the old man, and his own palm flat on the wet tile. These pictures feel more real to him than anything that happened yesterday. When his wife asks what he did at work today, he cannot recall the conversation he had with his manager about the new shipment schedule, but he can still feel the damp grit under his fingers as if it were pressing into his palm at that very moment. The shame that accompanies these images is almost unbearable—not shame about what he did, but shame about what he saw, as though witnessing others’ worst behavior made him complicit in it.

In the months after the explosion, Mark developed a set of quiet rituals to keep the pictures at bay. He tells himself, over and over, that the explosion did not really happen the way he remembers it, that he is exaggerating, that it was not that bad. He has said this so many times that a part of him almost believes it, until the texture of a slightly damp paper towel in the break room sends him back to the wet tile and the whole fragile structure collapses. He tries hard not to think about the event at all, shutting down any conversation that steers toward it, changing the TV channel when a news report shows a building damaged by fire. But the thoughts press in hardest when he is alone, especially at night, and it was during one of those sleepless nights a few months ago that he first took a box cutter to his forearm. The physical pain cut through the mental images, replacing the shame with something simpler. He has done it four times since, always in the same place, always when the snapshot of the wet tile or the red coat becomes too vivid to outrun by telling himself it didn’t happen.

His job has become a minefield. As a retail worker, he cannot avoid physical proximity to strangers; every customer who steps close to him at the register triggers a spike of vigilance. He has begun to interpret any abrupt movement or raised voice as the beginning of a stampede. When he sees a shopper argue with a cashier about a coupon, his chest tightens—people misbehaving, even in a trivial way, now feels like a precursor to disaster. He has asked his manager for more stockroom shifts, but the stockroom is where the memory of the wet tile lives most vividly, because the ceiling there has a similar texture. He cannot escape. His wife has noticed he is distant, that he flinches from her touch, that he laughs less. She does not know about the cuts. She has urged him to see someone, and after his most recent sleepless week he finally called a clinic.

What Mark is most afraid of, as he sits in the waiting room, is that the therapist will tell him the explosion really was that bad—because if it was that bad, then the shame, the pictures, the cutting, the desperate mental bargaining, none of it can be dismissed as overreaction. And if it was that bad, then he has to admit that the part of him which survived that afternoon is still back there, palm flat on the wet tile, waiting to be found. What he hopes for, though he cannot say it aloud, is that someone will help him turn those three frozen pictures back into a story he can walk away from.
